Hands on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis

Published

September 8, 2025

Modified

September 12, 2025

1 Overview

A spatio-temporal point process is a random collection of points representing the time and location of events such as diseases, species sightings, or natural disasters. With the rise of geographically and temporally indexed data, spatio-temporal analysis has become vital, supported by various R methods developed in the past decade. Using forest fire data from Kepulauan Bangka Belitung, Indonesia (Jan–Dec 2023), this study examines whether fire locations are spatially and temporally independent, and if not, where and when clustering occurs.

2 The data

In this Hands-on exercise, two data sets will be used as follows,

  • forestfires, a csv file provides locations of forest fire detected from the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) sensor data from Fire Information for Resource Management System.

  • Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung, an ESRI shapefile showing the sub-district (i.e. kelurahan) boundary of Kepulauan Bangka Belitung from Indonesia Geospatial portal.

3 Installing and Loading the R packages

Lets use six R packages for this hands-on exercise as follows,

  • sf provides functions for importing processing and wrangling geospatial data,

  • raster for handling raster data in R,

  • spatstat for performing Spatial Point Patterns Analysis such as kcross, Lcross, etc,

  • sparr provides functions to estimate fixed and adaptive kernel-smoothed spatial relative risk surfaces via the density-ratio method and perform subsequent inference. Fixed-bandwidth spatiotemporal density and relative risk estimation is also supported

  • tmap provides functions to produce cartographic quality thematic maps, and

  • tidyverse, a family of R packages that provide functions to perform common data science tasks including and not limited to data import, data transformation, data wrangling and data visualisation.

pacman::p_load(sf, terra, spatstat, sparr, tmap, tidyverse)

4b Converting OWIN

Now, as.owin() is used to convert kbb into an owin object.

kbb_owin <- as.owin(kbb_sf)
kbb_owin
window: polygonal boundary
enclosing rectangle: [512066.8, 705559.4] x [9655398, 9834006] units

Next, confirm if the output is an owin object.

class(kbb_owin)
[1] "owin"

5 Importing and Preparing Forest Fire data

We will import the forest fire data set and convert them to sf object.

fire_sf <- read_csv("data/forestfires.csv") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
                       crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32748)
Rows: 741 Columns: 15
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr   (3): satellite, instrument, daynight
dbl  (11): latitude, longitude, brightness, scan, track, acq_time, confidenc...
date  (1): acq_date

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

Convert data type of acq_date to numeric, because ppp object only accept numerical or character as mark.

fire_sf <- fire_sf %>% 
  mutate(DayofYear = yday(acq_date)) %>%
  mutate(Month_num = month(acq_date)) %>%
  mutate(Month_fac = month(acq_date, 
                           label = TRUE, 
                           abbr = FALSE))

6 Visualising the Fire Points

6a Overall plot

tm_shape(kbb_sf)+
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(fire_sf) +
  tm_dots()

6b Visuaising geographic distribution of forest fires by month

tm_shape(kbb_sf)+
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(fire_sf) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.1) +
tm_facets(by="Month_fac", 
            free.coords=FALSE, 
            drop.units = TRUE)

7 Computing STKDE by Month

Compute STKDE by using spattemp.density() of sparr package.

7a Extracting forest fires by month

Remove the unwanted fields from fire_sf sf data.frame because as.ppp() only need the mark field and geometry field from the input sf data.frame.

fire_month <- fire_sf %>% 
  select(Month_num)

7b Creating ppp

Derive a ppp object called fire_month from fire_month sf data.frame.

fire_month_ppp <- as.ppp(fire_month)

7e Plotting the spatio-temporal KDE object

plot() of R base is used to the KDE for between July 2023 - December 2023.

tims <- c(7,8,9,10,11,12)
par(mfcol=c(2,3))
for(i in tims){ 
  plot(st_kde, i, 
       override.par=FALSE, 
       fix.range=TRUE, 
       main=paste("KDE at month",i))
}

8 Computing STKDE by Day of Year

8a Creating ppp object

DayofYear field is included in the output ppp object.

fire_yday_ppp <- fire_sf %>%

fire_yday_owin <- fire_yday_ppp[kbb_owin]

9 Computing STKDE by Day of Year: Improved method

BOOT.spattemp() function supports bandwidth selection for standalone spatiotemporal density/intensity based on bootstrap estimation of the MISE, providing an isotropic scalar spatial bandwidth and a scalar temporal bandwidth.

By using BOOT.spattemp() function we can determine both the spatial bandwidth and the scalar temporal bandwidth.

set.seed(1234)
BOOT.spattemp(fire_yday_owin)

9a Computing spatio-temporal KDE

Now, the STKDE will be derived by using h and lambda values derive in previous step.

kde_yday <- spattemp.density(fire_yday_owin,
                             h = 9000,
                             lambda = 19)

Edge-correcting...Done.
